label: Claude Writing · Step 1
title: The Eight Tells
desc: What gives it away, sorted into categories that outlive the word lists.
text: 1 step 1 the eight tells what gives it away, sorted into categories that outlive the word lists. stop treating this as a vocabulary problem. the words are downstream. claude hedges because it was trained to be safe. it writes three-item lists because three-item lists score well on average. it uses transitions because it can't trust you to follow without them. fix the structure and most of the vocabulary fixes itself. every tell lands in one of eight categories. learn the categories, not the word lists. the specific words shift every few months. the categories haven't moved in three years. 1–3. the three waves of vocabulary the burned words. if these survive into a final draft, nobody edited it: delve, tapestry, testament, realm, landscape, paradigm, robust, leverage, utilize, facilitate, harness, unlock, elevate, foster, embark, underscore, multifaceted, holistic, seamless, paramount, meticulous, pivotal, crucial. the quiet wave. less obvious, equally fatal, and they leak across a whole draft: "that said," "at its core," "when it comes to," "in today's fast-paced world," "game-changer," "in the realm of," "by doing x, you can y," "whether you're a or b," "it's worth noting." the compensation wave. this is the 2026 one, and it fools people who know the first two lists cold. the models learned that the burned words get caught, so they overcorrect into manufactured casualness. "honestly," dropped in for false intimacy. "look," as an opener. "here's the thing:" as a transition. "hot take:" in front of an opinion the model doesn't hold. fake i-learned-this-the-hard-way stories with no specifics in them. 4. sentence-level tells the three-item compulsion: "innovative, scalable, and sustainable." two items or four would read more naturally. three scores better. "it's not just x, it's y." once per piece, maximum. "while x is true, y matters more." false balance, staged so the model looks even-handed before committing. em-dash chains — two or three per sentence — where a real writer uses one. rhetorical question answered on the spot. "does this matter? absolutely." cut the question. make the claim. sermon repetition: "we need speed. we need clarity. we need commitment." 5. structure tells a heading every 80 to 120 words. real writing runs further between signposts. bullets doing work that prose should be doing. bold scattered through the body. real bold is rare and earns its place. a "key takeaways" or "in summary" block bolted onto the end. trust the reader. every paragraph exactly three or four sentences. 6. rhetoric tells the hedge stack: "it's important to note that, in many cases, this could potentially..." both-sidesing. refusing to pick a winner when you asked for one. "it depends" with no framework behind it. vague benefits — "improved productivity," "better outcomes." if you can't put a number on it, it isn't a claim. 7. voice tells linkedin-guru shape: hook, three numbered lessons, motivational close. coach voice. "you've got this." "let's level up." fake vulnerability with nothing specific in it. real vulnerability has names, dates, and dollar amounts. tonal whiplash — a formal sentence sitting next to a forced-casual one. the clearest sign of a model trying to sound human. 8. punctuation micro-tells more than about one em-dash per 125 words. title case on every heading. perfect oxford comma compliance. people drift. models don't. en-dashes correct in every numeric range. almost nobody does that by hand. the one thing to remember readers don't catch ai writing by spotting a word. they catch it by rhythm — every sentence the same length, every paragraph the same shape, nothing at risk. you can strip every banned word on this page and still get caught if the cadence never changes.

label: Claude Writing · Step 2
title: The Banned List
desc: Cut on sight. This is the kill list.
headings: Soft ban — once per 1,000 words, maximum
text: 2 step 2 the banned list cut on sight. this is the kill list. none of these words are bad on their own. they're banned because they've been used so heavily that they now read as a handshake between one model and another. cut them unless you have a specific reason to keep one. banned words delve, leverage, utilize, facilitate, robust, seamless, paramount, multifaceted, holistic, ever-evolving, pivotal, crucial, meticulous, harness, unlock, elevate, foster, embark, underscore, arguably, notably, interestingly, ultimately, furthermore, moreover, additionally banned phrases "in today's fast-paced world" "it's important to note" "it's worth mentioning" "that said" "at its core" "when it comes to" "in the realm of" "navigate the landscape" "paradigm shift" "game-changer" "a tapestry of" "a testament to" "by doing x you can y" "whether you're a or b" "dive deep" "uncover insights" "unleash the power of" "at the end of the day" "it goes without saying" "in conclusion" soft ban — once per 1,000 words, maximum however. therefore. thus. hence. indeed. in essence. in summary. in short. plus significant , substantial , and notable any time there's no number attached to them. where this goes wrong banning words without changing structure trades one machine voice for another. strip every "furthermore" and inject "like, honestly" everywhere and you haven't fixed anything — you've cosplayed casualness. the fix is structural: shorter sentences, real specifics, real claims. tone follows.

label: Claude Writing · Step 4
title: The Six Laws of Human Prose
desc: Word swaps get you to neutral. These are what make writing sound alive.
headings: Law 1 — Specificity beats generality, every time
Law 2 — Rhythm has to vary or the prose dies
text: 4 step 4 the six laws of human prose word swaps get you to neutral. these are what make writing sound alive. everything in the two previous sections is subtraction. subtraction alone produces clean, competent, forgettable prose. these six laws are the addition side, and they're where the actual voice comes from. law 1 — specificity beats generality, every time numbers, names, dates, places, dollar amounts, exact quotes. "many companies struggle with hiring" is dead on the page. "we posted the pm role, interviewed 43 people, three of the top five turned us down over comp, filled it in six weeks from our own network" is alive. specificity is the cheapest and fastest signal that a person wrote this. law 2 — rhythm has to vary or the prose dies ai writes 15-to-18-word sentences at a metronome pace. people cluster: four words, eight words, thirty-two words, six words. vary the length, the opening, the structure. if you can clap a steady beat through three paragraphs, a machine wrote them. law 3 — make claims, take sides ai hedges because it was trained not to be wrong. people rank things, judge things, name names, and put their reputation behind it. every paragraph should carry at least one claim someone could argue with. law 4 — break rules on purpose fragments. sentences that open with a conjunction. one-word paragraphs. run-ons that build pressure. ai breaks rules by accident and inconsistently. people break them with intent, and the break carries the meaning. law 5 — show the friction real thinking is messy. writers reverse themselves mid-paragraph, drop a clause, leave a contradiction standing, end on a question. prose that's perfectly smooth and fully resolved reads as machine-finished. leave some seams visible. law 6 — lean into your obsessions ai writes about every subject the same way. you don't. you return to certain ideas, certain framings, certain words. don't sand that down. the repetitions are the voice. ten moves that inject voice one per 200 words is a reasonable baseline. add a number, name, or date. insert a contradiction. use an idiosyncratic word — load-bearing, the hinge, non-negotiable. drop a fragment after three full sentences. cite a real source by name. admit you don't know something. add a one-line aside in parentheses. use a temporal reference: "that was the saas-era playbook." repeat a word for emphasis. end on a question you haven't answered.

label: Claude Writing · Step 5
title: Teach Claude Your Voice
desc: Stop describing how you write. Make Claude derive it from what you've already written.
headings: Read it before you save it
Save it where Claude will actually read it
text: 5 step 5 teach claude your voice stop describing how you write. make claude derive it from what you've already written. most people try to explain their voice to claude in a sentence or two. "write it casual but professional." that produces nothing, because you're describing a feeling and claude needs patterns — how long your sentences run, how you open, how you sign off, the words you reach for and the ones you never touch. you already have thousands of samples of your own writing. point claude at them. the voice profile prompt connect gmail (or outlook), then run this once: read my last 30 sent emails in gmail. write my voice profile: how i greet, how i sign off, my sentence length, my go-to phrases, the words i never use. format it as writing instructions to follow when drafting as me. thirty is roughly the floor. below that claude picks up noise instead of pattern. sent mail beats anything else you could feed it, because it's writing you actually shipped to a real person under a real deadline, rather than writing you polished for an audience. read it before you save it the profile comes back as a list of observations, and this is the part people skip. read it. some of what it finds will be habits you don't want reinforced — i had a stretch of over-apologizing in email that claude dutifully wrote down as a signature move. delete those lines. what's left is your voice, minus the tics. save it where claude will actually read it a voice profile sitting in a chat window is worth nothing next week. put it in the file claude loads at the start of every session — the next section covers exactly where that lives and what else belongs in it. other sources worth feeding it sent email is the best single source, but not the only one. slack messages to your team catch how you write when you're moving fast. your last twenty linkedin posts catch your public register, which is usually different. if you write in two distinct modes — internal versus external — build two profiles and tell claude which one to use. already using this in a workflow the meeting follow-up engine in claude in action runs this same voice profile against meeting transcripts to draft recap emails that sound like you wrote them. build the profile here once, and that workflow gets better automatically.

label: Claude Writing · Step 6
title: Your Writing Rules File
desc: Set it once so you stop re-typing the rules in every session.
text: 6 step 6 your writing rules file set it once so you stop re-typing the rules in every session. or install the skill the voice-rules skill packages this guide's swap pass and structural pass, so you can say "use voice-rules on this draft." download stevesaiguide-skills.zip , then in claude go to customize , plugins , add , upload plugin . it holds two short skills and nothing else. run the five-minute check on it like any other plugin. everything above is worthless if you have to remember it each time. the point of a rules file is that claude reads it before it writes a word, every session, without you asking. where it goes a folder on your computer (desktop app): a claude.md file at the root of your project folder. loaded automatically at the start of every session in that folder. claude projects (web or mobile): paste it into the project's custom instructions. neither of those: keep it in a note and paste it at the top of any session where the writing matters. the starter block copy this whole thing. swap in your own voice profile from step 5 where marked. ## writing rules apply these to every draft you write for me. **banned words.** delve, leverage, utilize, facilitate, robust, seamless, paramount, multifaceted, holistic, ever-evolving, pivotal, crucial, furthermore, moreover, additionally **banned phrases.** "in today's fast-paced world," "it's important to note," "that said," "at its core," "when it comes to," "navigate the landscape," "paradigm shift," "game-changer," "by doing x you can y," "in conclusion" **four laws.** 1. specificity over generality. a number, name, or date in every paragraph. 2. vary rhythm. never three same-length sentences in a row. 3. make claims. take sides. name names. 4. cut connectors. use a period instead. **structure.** no "key takeaways" section. no heading every 80 words. no three-item lists by default. one em-dash per 125 words, maximum. **my voice.** [paste your voice profile from step 5 here] never tell me a draft is done. tell me what you'd cut next. the one-off version for a session where you don't want to set anything up, this does most of the work on its own: write [task]. hard rules: - no banned words: leverage, delve, robust, utilize, facilitate, seamless, paramount, holistic, pivotal, crucial - cut every "however," "furthermore," "moreover," "additionally" and use a period - vary sentence length wildly: at least two under 8 words, at least one over 25 - every paragraph needs a specific number, name, or date - no three-item lists. no "it's not just x, it's y." no rhetorical questions that you answer in the next sentence. - sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice. the line that does the most work "sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice." one sentence, and it fixes more than the whole banned list — because it's a target rather than a prohibition. claude is better at writing toward something than at avoiding things.

label: Claude Writing · Step 7
title: The Sniff Tests
desc: Twelve checks on a finished draft. None takes more than a minute.
headings: Have Claude grade its own draft
text: 7 step 7 the sniff tests twelve checks on a finished draft. none takes more than a minute. run these on anything going out under your name. most drafts fail two or three, and fixing those two or three is usually the whole job. test how to run it em-dash count per 500 words. ai averages 4–9, people average 1–3. over 5 means half need to become commas or periods. hedge count count "it's important to note," "however," "arguably," "could," "may," "in many cases" per 500 words. three or more is the ai hedge pattern. subject-first ratio how many sentences open with "the," "this," "it," or "our"? ai runs 60%+. people run 30–40%. reorder until you're under 50%. paragraph variance all paragraphs three or four sentences? that's the ai default. people cluster 1, 2, 5, 1, 7. connector density "furthermore," "moreover," "additionally," "in conclusion." one or more per paragraph reads as ai. adverb density words ending in -ly. ai runs 2–3 per paragraph. target 0–1. cut "significantly," "ultimately," "essentially," "basically" first. passive ratio "is / was / been / are" plus a past participle. ai runs 20–30%. target under 10%. three-item count count the "a, b, and c" lists. convert at least one to a pair, or split it into separate sentences. vague-noun audit "area," "space," "landscape," "realm," "domain," "opportunity" with nothing specific attached. each one needs a name, a number, or an example. claim-to-evidence ratio every claim should have evidence next to it — a number, a name, an anecdote. ai drifts to three claims per piece of evidence. the slack test paste a paragraph into slack to a colleague. would they reply "...what?" if so, it's too formal. the reorder test shuffle three paragraphs. if the new order reads as well as the old one, the prose has no rhythm. have claude grade its own draft score this draft against the twelve sniff tests in my writing rules. for each test, give the actual count and pass or fail. then rewrite only the sentences that caused the failures. don't touch anything that passed. the read-aloud test beats all twelve read the draft out loud at speaking pace. mark every sentence that trips you, sounds canned, or you'd never say to a person. rewrite those. it catches things no counting exercise will, and it takes about as long as the piece takes to read.

label: Claude Writing · Step 8
title: The Cheat Sheet
desc: One screen. Everything on this page, compressed.
headings: The prompt that does the most in one line
text: 8 step 8 the cheat sheet one screen. everything on this page, compressed. if you read nothing else here, read this. the nine-pass edit, in order don't try to fix a draft in one pass. cut before you add, structure before you polish. pass what you're hunting 1. hedge cut every weakening qualifier. if the sentence becomes a confident claim without it, the cut was right. 2. banned-word swap run the swap list. if there's no clean replacement, cut the sentence. 3. connector cull delete 60% of the "howevers" and "furthermores." replace with a period. 4. opening variation read the first three words of every sentence. three in a row starting the same way? rewrite one. 5. length burst add at least two sentences under 8 words and one over 28. 6. specificity injection every vague noun and metric-free claim gets a name, number, or date. 7. claim density every paragraph needs one arguable claim. pure-background paragraphs get folded in or killed. 8. voice injection one human signal per 200 words. a fragment, a contradiction, a specific story. 9. read aloud rewrite everything that trips. the four rules worth memorizing put a number, name, or date in every paragraph. never write three same-length sentences in a row. make a claim someone could argue with. cut the connector. use a period. the prompt that does the most in one line rewrite this so the final version is 30% shorter and 100% more specific. every sentence you cut was either hedging, repeating a claim, or adding no fact. sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice. the takeaway none of this makes claude write for you. it makes claude stop writing like claude, which is a different and more useful thing. the specifics still have to come from you — the number, the name, the thing that actually happened. claude can't invent those, and every tell on this page is really just claude covering for the fact that it doesn't have them. next step build your voice profile from step 5, paste it into the rules file in step 6, and run your next real draft through the sniff tests in step 7. that's about twenty minutes, and it's the last time you'll have to think about any of this. ← previous claude in office all guides next → claude everywhere claude writing by steve gustafson. how to stop claude sounding like claude, written by a human who edits a lot of drafts. updated october 2026 . back to all guides ↑

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 1
title: What Changed in July 2026
desc: One screen became three, plus a cloud underneath.
text: 1 step 1 what changed in july 2026 one screen became three, plus a cloud underneath. until july 2026, this kind of work lived on your desktop, in a mode then called cowork. if you wanted a scheduled task to fire, the mac had to be awake and the app open. close the laptop and everything stopped. the release changed three things at once. it now runs on mobile and web , not just the desktop app. sessions you start on your phone or the web run on anthropic's servers, so they keep going after you close the laptop. and scheduled tasks moved to the cloud , so they fire on time whether or not your computer is on. september 2026 closed the last seam. anthropic began merging that mode into ordinary chat, so on a merged account there is no switch to flip before you hand over a task. message box shows a chat / cowork switch? pick cowork for this. why . before and after before (desktop only) after (july 2026) one surface: the desktop app three surfaces: desktop, web, mobile scheduled tasks need the mac awake scheduled tasks run in the cloud, laptop closed a session lives on the machine you started it on cloud sessions sync to every device connectors set up per machine connectors shared across desktop, web, and mobile the one thing to remember not everything moved to the cloud. work that touches files on your actual computer still runs locally on the desktop. the next two sections are about telling the two apart, because that is where every confusion with this release comes from.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 2
title: And Then Chrome Joined (August 2026)
desc: Six weeks after mobile, the browser became a surface too.
text: 2 step 2 and then chrome joined (august 2026) six weeks after mobile, the browser became a surface too. six weeks after the july release, on august 12, 2026, the story picked up one more surface. claude in chrome stopped being a separate extension. the side panel became a full claude session, the same one you already run on desktop, web, and mobile. what that changes, in plain terms: skills and connectors work in the browser now. before august they did not. the chrome panel was a narrower tool that could see and click pages, and little else. work follows you across surfaces. start a task in a chrome tab at your desk, pick it up on your phone or your desktop with the full context. one session, a different screen. it is out of beta. chrome only, not edge, brave, arc, or mobile yet. since august 26, 2026 it is on every paid plan. enterprise admins manage it in organization settings and can restrict it to approved domains. why this is an "everywhere" update, not a browser feature chrome is the fourth surface now, next to desktop, web, and mobile, and it follows the same rule as the rest. a session you run in chrome is a cloud session, so it shows up on every device. the one-way mirror from the next section still holds: the cloud is visible everywhere, your local desktop work is not. the desktop app gained its own built-in browser on august 26, 2026. it is separate from your chrome and carries only the logins you bring over, site by site. it needs the desktop app. the safety trade-off because claude in chrome uses your existing logins, claude can reach anything you are signed into. since august 26, claude approves the actions it judges safe on its own, and a classifier checks each one against what you asked and blocks the ones that do not match. you can switch back to approving every action yourself in settings. keep only the tabs you want claude touching inside its group. for the full browser playbook, multi-tab research, form filling, scraping, and debugging, see claude advanced, chrome power moves .

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 3
title: The One-Way Mirror
desc: The mental model that keeps you out of trouble.
text: 3 step 3 the one-way mirror the mental model that keeps you out of trouble. there are two kinds of session behind the three screens. a cloud session is one you start on your phone or the web, plus every scheduled task. a local session is one you start on the desktop app, working inside a folder on your actual computer. sync runs one way. anything that happens in the cloud shows up everywhere: phone, web, and desktop. anything you do in a local desktop session stays on the desktop. your phone will never see it. say it like this the cloud is visible everywhere. your desktop is a one-way mirror: it can see the cloud, but the cloud cannot see it. who can see what where you started the work shows up on desktop? shows up on phone / web? phone or web (cloud session) yes yes scheduled task (cloud) yes yes desktop, inside a local folder yes no test it yourself start a session on your phone and watch it appear on the desktop. then do some local folder work on the desktop and check your phone. it won't be there. sixty seconds, and the model sticks for good.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 4
title: Cloud vs Local: Which Is Which
desc: Sort any task in five seconds.
text: 4 step 4 cloud vs local: which is which sort any task in five seconds. the question that decides whether a task runs with your laptop closed is simple: does it touch a file on your actual computer? if it only reads and writes connectors, it runs in the cloud. if it reaches into a local folder, it needs the mac. task type runs in the cloud? (laptop can be off) scheduled task reading gmail / calendar and writing a briefing yes a session you start on phone or web yes research that pulls from the web and a connector yes organizing or renaming files in a local folder no, needs the mac reading a local .xlsx or .docx off your desktop no, needs the mac the trap a task can be half-and-half: it reads gmail (cloud) but saves the output to a local "today's work" folder (desktop). that task runs fine, but the result only lands on your mac. you'll stare at your phone wondering where it went. the fix is the next section.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 5
title: Connectors Are the Bridge
desc: Where you store the output decides which devices can reach it.
text: 5 step 5 connectors are the bridge where you store the output decides which devices can reach it. this is the part the launch-day videos skip. because a cloud session can't touch your local folders, the only way to make a workflow's output reach your phone is to store it in a connector : google drive, notion, slack, gmail. the connector is the shared shelf all three surfaces can read from. that reframes connectors. they are no longer an optional step-nine nicety. they are the thing that decides whether your finished work follows you out of the building. the rule local folder output = desktop only. connector output = everywhere. if you want it on your phone, don't save it to your mac; save it to drive or notion. make your morning briefing portable a briefing that reads gmail and calendar is already pure-cloud. have it write the html to a google drive folder instead of a local one, and it lands on your phone at 8 am whether or not you opened your laptop. new to connectors? see claude beginner , section 9. "everywhere" has two meanings, and it decides your file format worth separating these before you build anything. you can open anything you drop in the cloud folder from your phone, html, markdown, whatever, using the drive or dropbox app. claude on your phone is stricter: the drive connector reads google docs, sheets, slides, pdfs, images, and office files. it does not read .md or .txt . so the briefing above is fine as html you read yourself, but if you want claude on your phone to pick a file back up and work with it, save it as .docx , .pdf , or a google doc. same reason your claude.md and memory.md stay a desktop concern, which is fine, the desktop reads them straight off the folder. checked against anthropic's google workspace connectors documentation, may 2026.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 6
title: Cloud-First or Local-First?
desc: A decision you make once per workflow.
text: 6 step 6 cloud-first or local-first? a decision you make once per workflow. every workflow you build now carries a design choice: should it live in the cloud so you can run and review it anywhere, or on the desktop where it has the full file tree? use this to decide. build it cloud-first when... build it local when... inputs and outputs live in connectors (email, calendar, drive, notion, crm) you're organizing, renaming, or reading files on your own machine you want to trigger it and review it from your phone the work is heavy file processing or code you watch run it's a scheduled task that should run while you sleep you want the full desktop workspace and local file tree write it into your claude.md set a storage default so you don't decide twice. something like: "outputs i want on mobile go to drive as .docx or pdf, never .md; local file-wrangling stays on the desktop." every future workflow inherits the right choice, format included.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 7
title: What Doesn't Work Yet
desc: Honest limitations, dated so you know when they expire.
text: 7 step 7 what doesn't work yet honest limitations, dated so you know when they expire. no hype here. as of july 2026, three gaps are worth knowing before you rebuild your whole setup around mobile. known limitations (as of july 2026) 1. web can't pick a local folder. the web app has no way to select a folder on your computer yet, so folder-based work still means the desktop. 2. local desktop work doesn't reach mobile. the one-way mirror. anything you do in a local session stays on the mac. 3. no promoting a local session to the cloud. you can't take a session you started on the desktop and continue it on your phone. start it in the cloud if you want it there. why the date matters anthropic is shipping fast. when one of these gets fixed, it's a one-line edit here, not a rewrite. check the date before you trust the limitation.

label: Claude Everywhere · Step 8
title: Rework Your Workflows for Mobile
desc: The same plays, now with a storage decision.
text: 8 step 8 rework your workflows for mobile the same plays, now with a storage decision. your existing workflows don't need replacing. they need one thing added: a storage decision, because storage now decides device reach. the 6 am dispatch, reborn the old version queued tasks from your phone for the mac to run. the new version runs the work itself in a cloud session, laptop closed, reviewable from any device. point its outputs at drive or notion instead of a local folder, and the finished work is on your phone with your coffee. full setup in claude in action , workflow 1. the essential three, freed morning briefing, meeting prep, evening debrief all read connectors and write a briefing. that makes them pure-cloud: they fire on schedule and land on your phone whether or not you opened your laptop. see claude in action , workflow 2. the takeaway the release didn't add new workflows. it changed where your existing ones can run and where their output can land. decide cloud or local per workflow, route mobile-bound output to a connector, and claude follows you across every screen. level up: audit your own setup tell claude: "list my scheduled tasks. for each, say whether it touches a local folder or only connectors, and flag the ones that need the mac awake. for anything i'd want on my phone, rewrite it to save output to drive instead of a local folder." ten minutes, and your whole automation layer knows which side of the mirror it's on. ← previous claude writing all guides next → claude plugins claude everywhere by steve gustafson. the mobile, web, and cloud side of claude, explained without the hype. updated october 2026 . back to all guides ↑

label: Claude Plugins · Step 1
title: What a Plugin Is
desc: Instructions plus access. The access is the part to watch.
text: 1 step 1 what a plugin is instructions plus access. the access is the part to watch. anthropic describes a plugin as a package that bundles skills, connectors, and sub-agents, so claude is set up for a job from the first conversation. plugins are on every paid plan, and they work in claude on the web and in the desktop app. the word "plugin" hides four different things. they do not carry the same risk. part what it is what it can touch skill written instructions claude follows for a task nothing by itself. it steers what claude does with the access claude already has. command a shortcut you type, like /monday-brief same as a skill. it starts one. connector a link to one of your accounts: gmail, drive, quickbooks whatever your own login can see and do in that account. local server or hook a small program that runs on your computer anthropic's wording: it runs "with the same permissions as any other program you run." the rule a plugin is as safe as the most powerful thing inside it. three skills and nothing else is a low-stakes install. three skills plus a connector to your email is a decision.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 2
title: Where Plugins Come From
desc: Four doors. Each one tells you how much checking was done before you arrived.
text: 2 step 2 where plugins come from four doors. each one tells you how much checking was done before you arrived. open customize in the sidebar, then the plugins tab. everything starts there. 1. the directory the discover tab. each listing names its publisher ("by anthropic", "by figma") and shows an install count. since september 25, 2026, new submissions go through anthropic's portal, where each one is validated and safety-scanned, then reviewed before it is listed. 2. a marketplace you add add , then add marketplace , then a repository address. this pulls plugins straight from someone's github. nobody reviewed them except the author. 3. a file someone sent you add , then upload plugin , which takes a .zip or .plugin file. the upload screen itself warns that anthropic has not checked the file. same trust level as an email attachment from that person. 4. one you build add , then create with claude . you know exactly what is in it, because you asked for it. the advanced guide covers building. review lowers the risk. it does not remove it. a directory listing passed a scan on the day it was approved. anthropic's own help page still says to install plugins only from sources you trust, and to review any plugin from outside anthropic before you turn it on.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 3
title: The Five-Minute Check
desc: Five questions before you click Add. None of them needs code.
text: 3 step 3 the five-minute check five questions before you click add. none of them needs code. 3.1 who published it? read the name on the listing and search for it. a company with customers, or a person with a public history, has something to lose. a name you cannot find anywhere else does not. 3.2 what is inside? open the listing and count the parts from step 1. skills and commands only: low stakes. a connector: read 3.3. anything that runs on your computer: stop unless you would let this publisher install software on your laptop. 3.3 what can it reach? name each account it connects. then finish this sentence: "if this plugin did the worst thing possible with that access, i would lose ___." if the blank is a client list or a bank login, the plugin needs to be worth it. 3.4 can you read it? skills are plain text files, usually a page or two. if the plugin lives on github, open them. you are looking for three things: instructions to send data somewhere, instructions to delete, and any line telling claude to ignore what you say. 3.5 what happens when it changes? a plugin can change after you install it. anthropic's help page says that when an author updates a shared plugin, recipients "automatically get the updated version at next use." the publisher you trusted on install day is the publisher you are trusting on every day after it. then run it carefully once first run: keep claude on manual so it asks before each action. for a plugin with no connectors, point it at a folder with nothing sensitive in it. for a plugin with connectors, the folder does not limit what it can reach, so read every action before you approve it, sends above all. a plugin that asks for more than its description promised fails the test.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 4
title: Choosing Connectors
desc: Thousands are listed. You need about five.
text: 4 step 4 choosing connectors thousands are listed. you need about five. the connectors tab listed 4,287 on october 5, 2026. four rules cover the choosing. prefer the one the service publishes. the gmail connector says "by google." the canva connector says "by canva." when the company that holds your data also wrote the connector, there is no third company in the middle. connect for a task, not for completeness. every connected account is one more place a bad instruction can reach. add a connector the day a workflow needs it. your existing permissions still apply. anthropic's small-business launch put it plainly: if an employee cannot see something in quickbooks or google drive today, they cannot see it through claude. disconnect what you stopped using. review the yours list once a quarter. step 8 shows how. why this matters more than it looks an attack needs three things at once: private data, untrusted content, and a way to send something out. one connector can supply all three. an email connector holds your private data, reads messages from strangers, and can send. the prompting guide, section 11 walks through the four habits that break the chain.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 5
title: Updates, and What Plugin4Shell Taught
desc: The plugin you installed in March is not guaranteed to be the plugin you are running in October.
text: 5 step 5 updates, and what plugin4shell taught the plugin you installed in march is not guaranteed to be the plugin you are running in october. on september 17, 2026, the security firm air security published a flaw it named plugin4shell. it affected four coding agents, claude code among them. whoever controlled a plugin's repository could swap in different code during an automatic update, while the setting meant to lock the plugin to one approved version appeared to hold. according to the report, anthropic fixed it in claude code 2.1.179. not every vendor had shipped a fix when the report came out. if you use the claude app and never claude code, this flaw did not reach you. the technical detail matters less than the three habits it argues for, and those apply to everyone. keep the app current. a fix only protects you if you have it. update claude code and the desktop app when they ask. install fewer plugins. each one is a publisher who can change what runs on your account. five plugins you use are safer than twenty you tried once. remove what you are not using. a plugin that is not installed cannot change underneath you.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 6
title: Claude Code Mods: Wait
desc: New in October 2026, and the most powerful thing a plugin can carry.
text: 6 step 6 claude code mods: wait new in october 2026, and the most powerful thing a plugin can carry. a mod is a small program, shipped inside a plugin, that changes how claude code itself works. it can rewrite a prompt, add a panel, or replace a built-in feature. mods arrived on october 1, 2026. mods are not sandboxed, anthropic says. they run with the same access to your machine as claude code, and its advice is to install them only from sources you trust, the way you would any software. for most readers of this guide if you only use the claude app, mods do not apply to you. if you use claude code, skip mods unless the publisher is anthropic or someone you would trust alone with your laptop while you are signed in. nothing in the other guides needs one.

label: Claude Plugins · Step 8
title: Turning One Off, Removing One
desc: Thirty seconds, and worth doing the moment you have a doubt.
text: 8 step 8 turning one off, removing one thirty seconds, and worth doing the moment you have a doubt. 8.1 turn it off first go to customize , then plugins , then yours . each plugin has a turn off button. off means claude stops using it, and you can turn it back on later. use this when you are unsure. 8.2 remove it same list. open the three-dot menu beside the plugin and choose remove . 8.3 close the doors it opened removing a plugin does not always disconnect the accounts it used. open the connectors tab, check yours , and disconnect any you no longer need. then remove claude's access inside the service too. for a google account, that list is under third-party connections in your account's security settings. 8.4 check what it left running open scheduled in the sidebar. delete any recurring task the plugin set up that you no longer want. the checklist before you add: who published it, what is inside, what it can reach, can you read it, what happens when it changes. first run on manual. turn a plugin off at the first doubt, and remove the ones you stopped using. sources anthropic help center, use plugins in claude anthropic, build plugins for claude , september 25, 2026 anthropic, claude for small business , september 15, 2026 anthropic, customize claude code with mods , october 1, 2026 air security, plugin4shell , september 17, 2026 ← previous claude everywhere all guides next → people i learn from claude plugins by steve gustafson. what a plugin can reach, and how to decide before you install one. updated october 2026 . back to all guides ↑
